candidate_sources.title: Leptographium Root Disease (Loblolly Pine Decline) - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Infected primary roots will have blue-stain and resin-soaked lesions caused by the Leptographium fungi (L. truncatum, L. procerum, L. terebrantis, L. serpens, and L. huntii). The disease results from the debilitation of root systems of stressed trees by Leptographium spp., which are vectored by various insects (Hylastes, Hylurgops, and Pachylobius species); these trees are very susceptible to southern pine beetles.

candidate_sources.title: Forest Health Guide for Georgia Foresters - Leptographium Root Disease of Loblolly Pine
candidate_sources.snippet: Many affected trees had thin, often tufted crowns that were slightly off-colored, with symptoms that closely resembled those associated with littleleaf disease. The disease results from the debilitation of root systems of stressed trees by Leptographium spp., vectored by root-feeding insects, leaving trees very susceptible to southern pine beetles.

candidate_sources.title: Pathogenicity of Leptographium Species Associated with Loblolly Pine Decline | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Seedlings inoculated with L. procerum produced significantly fewer root initials and a smaller root mass than control seedlings. Vertical lesions were produced in seedlings by L. serpens and L. terebrantis. Of the fungi tested, L. serpens, L. terebrantis, and L. lundbergii were the most aggressive and may pose the greatest threat to loblolly pines.

candidate_sources.title: AFC - Pine Decline
candidate_sources.snippet: Several root-inhabiting ophiostomatoid fungi, including Leptographium procerum, L. terebrantis, L. serpens, and Grosmannia huntii are associated with lateral root damage on declining loblolly pine. The fungi are vectored by root-feeding bark beetles and weevils and contribute to the decline of stressed loblolly pine.

candidate_sources.title: Pine needle rust | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Needle rusts in North America are caused by more than 20 species of the fungus Coleosporium. Closely related needle rusts also occur on other pines in this group, such as loblolly, Scots, shortleaf, and Virginia pines. Coleosporium is a heteroecious rust fungus, requiring two unrelated hosts. Symptoms consist of yellow spots on the needles in spring, followed by whitish blisters and orange spores. The fungus infects aster or goldenrod during summer. Management: remove wild asters and goldenrods near valuable pines.

candidate_sources.title: Pine Needle Rust : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Coleosporium asterum causes needles to develop reddish-orange dots on yellow spots or bands. A month later, flat-sided, white columns break open at the sides (aecia). Coleosporium asterum infects 2- and 3-needle pines. Alternate hosts include aster, goldenrod, and other Compositae. Management includes control of alternate hosts and good air circulation.

candidate_sources.title: Coleosporium needle rust of pine
candidate_sources.snippet: Coleosporium needle rust of pine. Caused by Coleosporium, a heteroecious rust requiring an alternate host (aster or goldenrod). Yellow spots on needles in spring followed by orange spore-producing pustules.

candidate_sources.title: Pine (Pinus spp.)-Needle Rusts | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Needle rusts of pine caused by Coleosporium species. Symptoms include yellow spots and orange spore-bearing pustules on needles. Alternate hosts include aster and goldenrod. Management and chemical control recommendations provided.

candidate_sources.title: FOR356/FR425: Red Heart Disease in Pines caused by Porodaedalea (Phellinus) pini in Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: Porodaedalea pini, more commonly known by its former names Phellinus pini and Fomes pini, is one of the most important wood-decaying fungi in pine forests, causing damage known as 'red heart' or 'red ring rot.' It primarily infects heartwood; reddish-brown decay with 'white pocket' and shelf-shaped conks. Preventing wounds during logging and pruning is the most effective management; no effective chemical treatment.

candidate_sources.title: Red Ring Rot (Porodaedalea pini) | UC Agriculture and Natural Resources
candidate_sources.snippet: Red ring rot (Porodaedalea pini) is a wood-decaying fungus that colonizes living trees but typically does not kill them, infecting heartwood and mechanically weakening the tree. Wounds are the primary route of new infection; red ring rot also creates wildlife habitat and complex forest structure.

candidate_sources.title: Forest Diseases in the Southeastern United States - Alabama Cooperative Extension System
candidate_sources.snippet: Heart rot damage is observed through hollows, rotten wood, irregular or lumpy stems, cankers, catfaces, scars, and fungus fruiting bodies (conks) on stems, often at the site of an old injury or branch removal. Covers wood decay and heart rot of southern pines including loblolly pine.

candidate_sources.title: Wood decay in living and dead trees: A pictorial overview (USDA Forest Service GTR-NRS-97)
candidate_sources.snippet: Wood-decaying fungi are traditionally classified as brown rot, white rot, or soft rot depending on the type of decay they cause. Pictorial overview of decay fungi and conks in living and dead trees.
